title: Some simple Turing machine computations require exponential effort

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Some simple Turing machine computations require exponential effort

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Exhaustive search of all roughly 4 billion 4-state 2-color Turing machines shows certain computations by such machines cannot be sped up by any machine of that size, suggesting that some computations specified by very simple rules require effort growing exponentially with input length.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: there are indeed Turing machine computations that cannot actually be carried out except by spending an amount of computational effort that can increase exponentially with the length of input.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Undecidability and Intractability” (from p. 753), p. 764. Scope: Turing machines with up to 4 states and 2 colors

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-24: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public computation can in principle reproduce the bounded exhaustive result, though it may exceed a small team's weeks-scale budget. The broader conclusion that the computations inherently require exponential effort is not implied by optimality within one machine-size class.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Exhaustively enumerate the stated four-state machine space, group machines by computed function, and compare minimum runtime growth within that bounded class. The finite-size optimality claim is confirmed by exhaustive equivalence checks; an unrestricted exponential lower bound requires a separate proof.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Optimality among four-state machines does not prove optimality among all algorithms.

Finite input samples do not establish exponential asymptotics.

Four billion machines make full replication resource-intensive.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The finite half of the claim is a definite enumeration of about four billion rules, large but reproducible with a careful implementation. What that search can show is that no machine of the same size speeds up the cited examples. The further suggestion that very simple rules require exponential effort in general is a lower bound, and public busy-beaver data answer a different question about blank-tape halting.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Re-enumerate four-state two-color machines and test whether any computes the same function as the cited examples in subexponential maximum time. That decides the no-speedup-within-this-size clause. A lower bound against machines of every size is a separate proof the census does not provide.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Inputs that run off the left must be separated from inputs that are merely very slow.

An exponential lower bound against all machines is an open complexity proof.

A search at four states shows the absence of a faster machine only inside that size bound.
